# ProbOS — Architectural Decisions

Append-only log of architectural decisions made during ProbOS development. Each AD documents the reasoning behind a design choice.

See [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md) for project status. See [docs/development/roadmap.md](docs/development/roadmap.md) for future plans.

**Archives:** [Era I — Genesis](decisions-era-1-genesis.md) | [Era II — Emergence](decisions-era-2-emergence.md) | [Era III — Product](decisions-era-3-product.md) | [Era IV — Evolution](decisions-era-4-evolution.md)

---

## Era V — Civilization (Phases 31-36)

> **A recurring defect shape, named once here because it appeared SEVEN times in two days (2026-07-27/28): a mechanism is built and tested, and the thing that would exercise it never does.** AD-1157 (a classification field no caller supplied — 2,453/2,453 records took the default), BF-688 (a priority parameter every handler omitted), BF-690 (a guard armed while the offered schema still advertised the refused actions), BF-692 (element discovery guarding a Playwright method that does not exist), BF-695 (the entire browser tool could not start on Windows), AD-1162 (AD-1158's session binding read a context key nothing produced), BF-696 (a boot race needing two things to interleave).
>
> In every case the tests passed, because **the test double was more capable than production** — a fake `page` implementing `list_elements`, a test supplying the very key it was meant to prove arrives from elsewhere. BF-695 was worse than invisible: `asyncio_mode="auto"` runs the suite on `ProactorEventLoop` while production runs on `WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy`, so the suite was exercising the opposite loop from the one that ships.
>
> **The forcing question is: name the real caller. Not the test — the production path.** Four of these seven die on it immediately. The rest need: does the double implement something the real object does not, and has this path ever executed on a live runtime? A unit test of a mechanism structurally cannot see this class of bug.

### AD-1291 (2026-08-29) - one device, one owner (BF-858, #1328)

**The defect is a mutual-cancellation CASCADE, not a truncation, and the correction matters because it changes what an acceptance test may assert.** Seven live speech producers share one audio output. `voice.ts` emits the terminal `'end'` carrying the **superseded** utterance's id (BF-767), and the BF-764 arrival drain correlates on exactly that id — so a foreign producer's cancel did not merely cut the current utterance, it **resolved the drain and advanced it**, launching the next utterance on top of the interloper. BF-764's own correlation guard is the propagation mechanism. Three utterances, none heard whole, and the transcript still ends in the right order. **Any test checking only the final spoken array therefore passes against the unfixed code** — the two end-to-end spans assert non-overlap instead, and were verified red against the unfixed behaviour before being trusted.

**Decision: a deterministic `SpeechArbiter` at module level in `ui/src/audio/voice.ts`.** Under AD-1231 the boundary test is *who decides what*. The audio device is a single physical resource with a hard concurrency bound of one; "only one utterance occupies the speaker", "utterances start in admission order", "each completion is delivered exactly once" are **guarantees**, not judgements — the class AD-1231 assigns to a deterministic service. Seven producers cannot promise that by negotiation, and the cascade is what their negotiation actually produced. It lives in `voice.ts` and **not** in the chat component because `IntentSurface` is mounted at `App.tsx:113` for the whole session, concurrently with `ProfileChatTab`, and both reach the same module state — which also settles the issue's own open question. A component-level queue cannot see a sibling's producer, and span 2 is the test that proves it.

**The prohibitions are the load-bearing part.** The arbiter may not decide *whether* an utterance is worth saying (that stays with the BF-718 claim ledger), may not rank or reorder by content, topic, importance or agent, may not attribute, may not dedup, may not read or rewrite text, and may not consult trust, Hebbian weights, attention or any LLM. Its **only** non-FIFO input is a two-valued class **declared by the caller** — `interactive` pre-empts `narration`, strict FIFO within a class. Choosing the class is the producer's decision ("what kind of thing am I saying"), which keeps the cognitive half with the caller and leaves the arbiter with ordering and delivery only. An arbiter that inferred the class by inspecting the text would be deciding what is worth saying, which is the AD-1231 violation this shape exists to avoid.

**A `narration` pre-empted by an `interactive` utterance is dropped, and the drop is justified rather than convenient.** The test is *does the channel still carry the information* — narration by construction narrates text already rendered in the visible transcript, so dropping it loses the audio rendition, not the content. Speaking it *after* the live turn would narrate stale text as though current, which actively misleads about ordering. Any drop failing that test is forbidden, which is exactly why an `interactive` utterance is **never dropped by pre-emption**: nothing else carries it. Everything else queues. **The invariant is scoped to pre-emption deliberately, and adversarial review caught the unscoped form of this sentence overclaiming.** `flushSpeechQueue` — barge-in and tab unmount — drops queued-but-unstarted entries of *either* class, because both are the Captain (or the UI) saying *stop*, not the arbiter deciding one utterance matters less than another; honouring that is the whole point of barge-in, and preserving an interactive backlog across it would resume speech the Captain just interrupted. The in-flight entry is left alone so its consumers still receive the terminal `'end'`. **Every drop on every path emits an observable `dropped` event with a reason — there are no silent drops.**

**The contract that keeps nine existing consumers working: id at enqueue, audio at dispatch, events at audio.** `speakResponse` still returns its id **synchronously**, because the BF-764 drain and BF-290 both capture it and correlate before awaiting. `'start'`/`'end'` still fire **only when audio actually plays**, because `wakeWord` and the BF-300 PTT gate use them to gate the **microphone** — announcing an utterance at enqueue time would mute the Captain while the room is silent, a worse defect than the one being fixed. `undefined` continues to mean only "no engine exists"; a queued utterance returns a real id. `dropped` is additive, and was verified inert against all nine subscribers, every one of which filters on `type`.

**`stopSpeaking` now flushes the queue, because the fix would otherwise introduce a regression in its own seam.** Before the queue, barge-in stopped the utterance and nothing followed. With a queue, cancelling would immediately dispatch the next — so the Captain gets talked over by a backlog at the exact moment they try to speak. Wired into `stopSpeaking` rather than at each call site because every barge-in path already funnels through it, so no future caller can forget. `wakeWord.ts:187` needed no change: contrary to the build prompt, that subscription only sets the `_bargedIn` suppression flag and never cancels anything.

**Two defects were introduced during the build and are recorded because both were invisible to reasoning and caught only by the existing suite.** (1) Moving BF-764's `SPEECH_JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS` into `voice.ts` — as the prompt directed — put a constant behind a module ~20 test files replace with a `vi.mock` factory; the factory does not define it, **Vitest's proxy throws on access**, and the throw landed inside the drain's promise executor, killing the loop after one utterance and silencing every later message. The constant stays local. (2) Clearing the active-utterance token on the arbiter's completion killed AD-1071 sentence pipelining after sentence one, because every sentence of a reply shares the reply's id (BF-767). The token is now handed over by the next dispatch and cleared by `stopSpeaking`, never by completion. The AD-1071 predicate correspondingly asks "do I still own the device" rather than "is my id the newest" — under the arbiter `_speakGeneration` advances at **enqueue**, so the old test would have let a merely *queued* reply truncate the reply actually playing.

**The BF-764 component drain was deliberately NOT deleted, against the prompt's Section 3.** Section 3 and §4.1 contradict each other: §4.1 names that drain as "the consumer that must accept this change… the strictest, because it captures the synchronous return, correlates `'end'` on it, and carries both guards", and a change cannot be validated against a consumer it deletes. Keeping it was verified correct rather than merely tolerable — with both queues in series the send path still enqueues without dispatching, and non-overlap holds. Deleting it would have forced the 12 BF-764 tests onto a fake-arbiter mock, and two of them (GUARD 1, GUARD 2) would then assert the **fake's** guards while production never ran — green tests proving nothing, which the standing order forbids. Both guards are re-tested for real against `voice.ts`. The redundant inner queue is left as a separate cleanup.

**Deliberately not changed.** The BF-718 claim ledger still decides *whether* to speak. The AD-921 reveal clock still owns meeting pacing — the sequencer becomes an ordinary client that can no longer be cancelled mid-sequence. `defersToMeetingSequencer` stays; it selects who narrates a group room, which is routing, not device ownership. BF-767 id semantics are unchanged. **`meetingVoice.ts:118` is left alone**: a bare `'end'` with no `agent_id` matches any reply, so a Ship's Computer utterance can still advance the meeting sequencer early. It is independently reachable, unchanged by the arbiter, and belongs in its own BF.

### AD-1284 (2026-08-29) - the consensus gate must be reachable, and its absence declared (BF-779, #1242 findings 1 & 2)

**Finding 2 was worse than the issue stated, and the enumeration is what found it: `mcp_invoke`'s consensus gate was INERT on the plan path.** The DAG executor special-cased exactly one intent **by name** (`node.intent == "write_file"`); `device.*` escapes that by having a dispatch bridge, the tree's only consensus intent-bus subscriber; `mcp_invoke` had neither. So a decomposed `{"intent": "mcp_invoke", "use_consensus": true}` took the generic path, `McpConsensusProposer` returned a proposal (it never invokes, by design), quorum was evaluated — and **nothing called `MCPBridge.invoke`**. Built, tested, and reachable only from the MCP workbench. It failed safe, which is why it survived: no unauthorised invocation, just a capability that could not be used. Reproduced red before the fix — a one-node DAG with an APPROVED quorum committed **0** times where 1 was required.

**The issue's own headline had drifted and is corrected.** *"`write_file` is the only intent that gets a real gate"* was true when filed; re-enumerated at `b96e3b1d` there are **four** `submit_*_with_consensus` methods and **three** commit only on APPROVED (`write_file`, `mcp_invoke`, `device_actuate`). `commit_write` remains the only agent-side commit method in the tree.

**Decision: neither a fourth special case nor a universal propose-then-commit protocol.** Both were rejected for the same reason read from opposite ends. A **universal protocol** fails because one population physically cannot satisfy it: `run_command` does `subprocess.Popen` inside `handle_intent`, `run_python` runs a sandboxed script, `install_package` pips into a venv — the act **is** the observation, and a "proposal" would be a no-op announcing an intention. Forcing a `commit_` method on them yields a ceremonial proposal followed by unconditional execution, which is a gate in name only — **the exact defect BF-779 was filed about**, re-introduced as ceremony. A **fourth special case** fails because §1 shows the special cases *are* the problem: one name in one `if` is why `mcp_invoke` was dead.

**So: (1) reachability — a runtime-owned `gated_commit_for(intent)` table replaces the name check**, registering `write_file` and `mcp_invoke`, which closes the inert path and deletes the special case in one move. "Which intents have a real gate" becomes one enumerable fact instead of knowledge spread across a decomposer `if`, a subscriber list and three docstrings that disagreed. **`device.*` is deliberately absent from the table** — it already commits through its bridge and needs a parameter translation the uniform `(params)` shape cannot express; adding it would give one commit two dispatch routes. **(2) Declaration — `IntentDescriptor.consensus_mode`** in `{propose_commit, execute_then_vote, external_gate}`. `requires_consensus` says a vote happens; this says whether the vote **authorizes** the act.

**The default is `execute_then_vote`, chosen because it is the unflattering one.** A new consensus intent that declares nothing is reported as ungated rather than presumed safe, and no existing descriptor changes behaviour. Six intents declare `propose_commit`; `build_code` declares `external_gate` (it is broadcast directly at `routers/build.py` and gated by Captain approval — declaring that describes it, it does not change it). `shell_command`, `code_runner` and `skill_framework` are **deliberately left on the default**: it already states the truth about them, and an explicit restatement would only create a second place to drift.

**The runtime records and warns; it never refuses.** One startup warning names every `requires_consensus=True` intent still on `execute_then_vote`, and `intent_resolved` rows plus the returned dict now carry `consensus_mode` — an unregistered intent reports `"unknown"` rather than a fabricated mode. Previously an operator reading that row could not tell whether the recorded quorum authorised the act or merely scored it, which is precisely how "consensus-gated" became folklore about intents that were never gated. **Refusing was rejected under Design Principle #13(c)**: blocking `run_command` would remove a capability while defending nothing, because the vote it would be "enforcing" never authorised anything. It is a warning because the gap is real, and not an error because for that population the gap is irreducible.

**Finding 1 is explicitly NOT "make the generic path roll back."** It cannot: that population has nothing to roll back to. Its honest resolution is that everything gateable is routed to a gate and everything else is declared and logged as such.

**A test-double class of defect surfaced and is recorded, because only one of five instances failed loudly.** `MagicMock(spec=ProbOSRuntime)` auto-mocks `gated_commit_for` into a **truthy** Mock, so a spec'd double routes a consensus node down the commit path and then raises on `await`. Five sites in `test_escalation.py` were affected; **one failed and four kept passing for the wrong reason** — the TypeError escalated, the escalation resolved, and the assertions still held while the test no longer exercised consensus rejection at all. The doubles were corrected to return `None` as the real method does for `read_file`/`run_command`. A guard that tolerated a non-coroutine gate was considered and **rejected**: it would fail open, silently returning an intent to the ungated path, which is BF-779 coming back quietly.

**Mutation: 16 killed, 2 null controls survived, 0 inert, 0 invalid** — after two corrections that are the more useful result. One surviving mutant was the **mutant** being wrong, not the test: it changed only the warning's wording (`BF-779` → `BF-779-muted`), which the assertion's substring filter still matched. One went **inert** because a 12-space anchor is a *substring* of the 16-space line above it; whole-line matching fixed it. Both are reported as corrected rather than as coverage.

**Deliberately not built.** No gate for `run_command` / `run_python` / `install_package` — the Captain's BF-763 decision stands and AD-1278/1280's per-execution audit record is the control there, its "attempted / UNCONFIRMED" language unchanged. `docx_create` / `docx_revise` / `pptx_create` / `xlsx_update` are **not** converted to propose-then-commit; that is four adoptions, not an architectural correction. `submit_intent_with_consensus` keeps its shape, the `device.*` bridge is untouched, the MCP workbench wiring is untouched (the DAG now reaches the same method by a second entry point, not a second commit), and no trust, Hebbian, Shapley or red-team behaviour changes.

### AD-1283 (2026-08-28) - what termination owns (BF-861, #1331)

AD-1278 made the persisted audit chain hole-free: an entry that cannot enter the write queue **spills** rather than dropping, because a dropped sequence leaves the next persisted row's `prior_hash` pointing at an absent predecessor — a chain that reports `broken` at every future boot. #1331 is the price of that guarantee. The spill was unbounded, and once the durable stream terminated `max_entries` stopped applying at all: nothing above `_persisted_through` is evictable, and a terminated stream never advances that watermark again. Measured on HEAD, wedged sink, 5,000 appends at a cap of 3: **`len(entries) == 5000`**.

**Decision: `_terminate_stream` DISOWNS what the writer is holding, instead of waiting for the writer to hand it back.** Termination already meant "no further entry is enqueued"; it now also means "the log no longer accounts for the in-flight batch." The eviction predicate is then `_stream_broken_at is not None` **alone** — true the instant termination happens, with no dependency on writer liveness. The disowned batch keeps its own reference and may still commit; if it does, the disk chain simply ends one batch later, still contiguous.

**Two earlier attempts were rejected, and both were wrong in the same way.** Round 1 let `_enforce_cap` evict once the stream was terminated; review raised a High, that the ceiling terminates from the *append* path while the writer may still hold a persistable batch. Round 2 applied the prescribed guard — evict only when `_inflight == 0 and not self._retry_batch` — and review raised a new High: against a permanently wedged writer `_inflight` never returns to zero, so the gate never opens and growth is unbounded again (measured 2,020 entries). Both rounds asked *"when is it safe to evict?"* and answered *"once the writer lets go,"* which makes the memory bound depend on the liveness of the one component already known to be stuck. **A bound that waits on a wedged component is not a bound**, and round 2 reproducing the defect it was fixing is the signature of a wrong question rather than an unfixed bug.

**The premise both rounds shared is false, and the reviewer's own measurement refutes it read the other way up.** `_next_batch` builds `batch: list[AuditEntry]` as its own list, `AuditEntry` is frozen, and `_evict` does `del self.entries[:count]` — so eviction drops list **slots**, not entries, and cannot reach the writer's batch at all. Probed against the round-1 build with the sink released afterwards: sequence 0 was evicted from `entries` (`entries=[17, 18, 19]`, `truncated_at=(16, …)`) and **still landed on disk** (`disk=[0]`). There was never anything to protect. `test_eviction_does_not_take_the_in_flight_batch_off_the_disk` pins this so a future "protect the writer" gate cannot come back.

**Terminating at the ceiling is kept; the alternatives are worse, enumerated.** Dropping from the spill **head** is precisely the hole BF-780 exists to prevent. Dropping from the **tail** is behaviourally identical to terminating except that it lies — `durable_stream_open()` keeps returning True while nothing is written. **Backpressure** contradicts the module's stated contract, that making the sink a precondition "would turn the accountability trail into a new way to lose work." A **second spill file** adds a second durability surface with its own failure modes while the first is wedged. Growing for ever is the defect. Neither review finding was about the ceiling; both were about what termination leaves behind. **Cancelling the writer** was also rejected: the bound it appears to deliver is actually delivered by the accounting reset bundled with it, `task.cancel()` lands only at the next await so a genuinely hung `persist_entries` may never receive it, and it buys a literal docstring at the cost of a cross-task race. A **grace period** does not remove unbounded growth; it rate-limits it, and puts a timer in a synchronous `append` path.

**Two further defects, both introduced by the ceiling and missed by both review rounds.** (a) **`_terminate_stream` was not idempotent.** With two call sites the second overwrites the first, and this number is what an operator reads to learn where the on-disk chain ends. First termination now wins. (b) **The ceiling's reported sequence overstated durability.** Terminating also drains and discards the **queue**, whose sequences sit *below* the spill's, so naming `spill[0].sequence` claims those queued sequences reached disk. Reproduced as a red test: `broken_at=2` while sequence 1 was discarded and disk ended at 0. It reports `_persisted_through + 1` instead — provably the same quantity the refusing-sink call site already passes, since `persist_entries` is all-or-nothing and `_advance_persisted` walks contiguously.

**A claim in the build prompt was false and is corrected here.** The prompt derived (a) from a measurement of the ceiling firing at 2 and a later refusal moving it to 0 — but that backwards move is an **artefact of (b)**. Measured on the fixed build, the two call sites converge: ceiling 0 then refusal 0 on a cold log, 1 then 1 after one confirmed batch, with `batch[0].sequence == _persisted_through + 1` in both. The guard is still load-bearing, in the **opposite** direction: an under-reporting sink makes `_advance_persisted` refuse the jump, so the watermark stalls while the writer's batch head climbs, and a later refusal would report **4** where the ceiling correctly reported **1** — claiming sequences 1–3 reached disk. That is the reachable case, and it is pinned by its own test rather than by the simple scenario, which the other half of the fix masks.

**Mutation finding worth recording: the disown's only unmasked effect is `_unflushed()`.** `_enforce_cap` keys on termination alone and never reads writer state, and `_await_quiescent` has its own terminated-stream early return, so removing `self._inflight = 0` left every behavioural test green. What it does change is that `drain` would report a phantom tail for a writer it can never resolve — a **second** loss report for a loss `_terminate_stream` has already announced, with a different cause. That is now pinned. `self._retry_batch = []` has, at this HEAD, no unmasked effect at all (its one reader is the masked branch in `_await_quiescent`); it is kept because it makes termination's accounting self-consistent, and is recorded here as unpinned rather than left to look tested.

**Deliberately not built.** No writer cancellation, no timer or grace period, no change to the retry path, `mark_persisted_through`, `verify_chain`, `chain_state`, `mark_truncated`, `durable_stream_open()` or the shutdown sequence. `spill_maxsize <= 0` restores the pre-BF-861 unbounded buffer, documented as the opt-out.

### AD-1275 (2026-08-28) - composition belongs to the agent-role sink (BF-806, #1270)

Model-authored replies reached stored, Captain-visible transcript rows with the AD-722a `<intent emotion=NAME>` self-tag and `[A2UI]{json}[/A2UI]` blocks intact. BF-792 built one shared `compose_bypass_reply` and wired it into two modules; an enumeration of the writers into `ChatThreadStore` found **eleven**, and reached the `cognitive_agent` work-item acknowledgement to get a stored body carrying both markers.

**Decision: composition happens ONCE, at the sink, for `role == "agent"` rows — inside `ChatThreadStore.append_message_once`. A model-authored row wearing a non-agent role is a producer-side obligation, and there is exactly one of them.**

**Why the producer-side answer loses.** It has now been tried three times: BF-702 fixed one marker on one path, and BF-791/BF-792 found the other three cells. It requires the author of a *future* writer to know the obligation exists. An enumeration test makes them notice, but noticing is not doing, and the test cannot tell a correct classification from a lazy one. The DM egress reached this conclusion first and it is already written into `dm_reply.py`: *"six review rounds proved a hand-written sink list is not [enforceable]: it was wrong every round, and the last one found a pseudo-sink hiding seven real ones."* BF-806 is that finding one layer down — the eleven-module list in #1270 was itself wrong on first draft, and the test found three modules the review's own enumeration had missed.

**Why the sink can be trusted, and it is one fact rather than a judgement call.** `append_message_once` holds the sole `INSERT INTO chat_thread_messages` in the tree, and `role` is a **required, closed-set, sink-validated parameter** — a row is rejected outright unless `role in {"captain", "agent", "system"}`. So a rule keyed on author role is not an inference the store has to make; the discriminator is already an argument it refuses rows for getting wrong. Measured rather than assumed: an AST census of all 22 `append_message*` call sites across 11 modules found the role known at the sink for **every** row — 20 pass a literal, one is internal delegation, one is a REST field constrained by `pattern="^(captain|agent|system)$"`.

**The sink reads the role and never sniffs the body, and that is what makes the rule safe rather than clever.** A `role="captain"` row is stored **byte-identically**, without exception: if the Captain literally types `[A2UI]{...}[/A2UI]` or an emotion tag, it is his text. A marker-shaped string is not evidence of provenance, and treating it as such would corrupt exactly the content this work exists to protect. `role="system"` is likewise untouched — every system body is a hardcoded literal, so there is nothing to strip, and leaving it alone keeps the rule "exactly one role is composed" rather than "two roles, for different reasons".

**The one hole, and why it is the only one.** `cognitive_agent` posts a work-item title/description as `role="captain"`. Those fields come from the work item, and **agents create work items**, so the body is model-reachable while the row is indistinguishable at the store from a message the Captain typed — same role, same `author_id`, same shape. No sink rule can clean it without also rewriting genuine Captain text. It is therefore composed at the producer, and Slice A alone does not close #1270 without it.

**Empty-after-composition is a decided policy, not a fallthrough.** A body that was nothing but markers composes to `""`. The store must not insert a blank bubble and must not return `None` — `crew_executor` reads `None` as a missing thread and would report a false `crew_execution_message_thread_missing`. So a non-empty agent body that composes to empty is stored as a named constant and logged at `warning`. A body that was **already** empty is left byte-identical: that is the caller's own choice, not a body composition consumed. The two already-wired producers each supply their own empty-reply wording before reaching the store, so a producer with an opinion still wins; the constant only covers producers that do not.

**Ordering inside the method is load-bearing.** Composition lands after the type validation (so `type(body) is not str` still rejects first) and **before** the idempotency comparison `current.body == body`. Placed after it, a crew re-offer of the same `message_id` would compare a composed row against a raw argument and raise `chat_thread_message_conflict` on a correct retry.

**Function-scope import, deliberately.** `threads/__init__.py` declares stdlib-only module-scope dependencies. A module-scope edge to `probos.cognitive` would make a persistence module import a cognitive one — a layer violation — and would pull `a2ui` and `artifacts` into every process that opens a thread store. The idiom already exists in this file (`suggest_title`). There is no `try/except` around the import or the call: a failure there is a programming error, and degrading to "store it raw" would reinstate the defect while every producer's own `except Exception` hid the evidence.

**Rejected: constructor injection.** One production construction site against 166 in tests; a `None` default would mean the suite exercises the non-composing path, which is precisely the gap being closed. The `set_message_committed_callback` / `_clock` / `_id_factory` precedent in this class is real but does not apply — those are optional observers and seams, whereas this is a contract the store must always honour. An injectable egress rule is an egress rule you can forget to wire.

**Rejected: refusing the row.** Turning `RenderedDmText` / `require_rendered` into a store admission token would raise into seven producer `except Exception` blocks and turn a visible marker into a silently dropped reply — strictly worse for the Captain. Transform, do not refuse.

**The guard was re-purposed, not weakened, and the vacuity trap was real.** `_COMPOSED_SINKS` now means "composes at the producer because its row is not `role="agent"`" and `_OTHER_SINKS` means "covered by the sink, or exempt". The enumeration scan and both of its failure directions are unchanged. But `test_the_composed_sinks_actually_import_the_composition` walks only `_COMPOSED_SINKS`, and the writer scan matches `append_message` call sites that survive any deletion — so with the sink edit removed the entire guard file stayed **green**. One assertion closes that: the sink module itself must reference `compose_bypass_reply`. Verified by mutation — stripping both references reddens exactly that test and nothing else.

**Deliberately not built.** No composition added to the eight `role="agent"` producers — the sink covers them, and a producer-side call would re-create the per-path pattern this AD retires. No change to `DmReplyPipeline` or `step_4k_extract_a2ui`: the shipped interactive widget is unaffected, because `replace_a2ui_with_stubs` leaves `[A2UI: name vN - kind]` and `_MARKER_PROBE` requires the literal `[A2UI]` — pinned by a test that also transforms a raw block in the same body, so the byte-identity assertion cannot pass vacuously. No relocation of `compose_bypass_reply` to a leaf module. No change to `routers/threads.py`, its role pattern, or the UI.

### AD-1278 (2026-08-28) - the record that replaced the gate has to outlive the process (BF-780, #1243)

BF-763 removed the quorum gate on `run_python` on the explicit argument that the per-execution audit record **is** the substitute control. That record was best-effort in four ways at once: an in-memory list, a sink shipped OFF, no shutdown drain, and unbounded growth with one `asyncio` task per append. If the record can be absent, the substitution failed and the gate was removed for nothing.

**Decision: durable-preferred with honest degradation, not durable-required.** Recorded with its cost, per Design Principle 13(a).

**The counter-argument taken seriously.** Durable-required — refuse to execute when the sink is unavailable — is not ruled out by 13(a): chosen deliberately and shipped with the default already on, it would be a *decision*, not an inheritance. Nor is it ruled out by 13(c). 13(c) is about the **chain of command** — an agent that cannot authorise something escalates rather than refusing — and its remedy is *routing*. A locked SQLite file has nobody to escalate to. **13(c) is off-point here and must not be cited as the reason.**

**What actually decides it, in order of force.** (1) **Durable-required does not deliver what it promises.** A sink check happens at *launch*; all four gaps are about a record lost *after* a successful `append` — an undrained tail at shutdown, an eviction, a queue overflow, a crash. A launch-time check proves the sink existed at t=0 and proves nothing about whether *this* record survives. It buys the appearance of guaranteed accountability at real availability cost while leaving the drain and the cap exactly where they are: the more rigorous-sounding option and the less rigorous one. (2) **DP 13(b): prefer a governed path over a removed one.** Durable-required buys accountability by deleting the capability, and it would silently reverse a decision already shipped and reasoned about in this very module — `execution/audit.py` swallows sink exceptions precisely because *"an audit write that could fail an execution would turn the accountability trail into a new way to lose work."*

**The answer to "then the gate was removed for nothing."** It was removed **in exchange for a record**. The way to honour that exchange is to make the record survive, which is what this AD builds: the sink is now the shipped default (`audit_persistence_enabled: true` in both the model and `config/system.yaml`), shutdown drains the writer before exit, `entries` is bounded, and appends go through one queue with one writer instead of one task each.

**"Preferred" is only honest if degradation is visible.** It was not: the notice was a `logger.warning` fired once per auditor instance into a log nobody reads. So `ExecutionAuditor.record` now **returns** what it can actually observe. The first attempt at this returned `"durable"`, decided from pre-append conditions — sink present, writer open, queue not full — and wrote that answer into the record as `detail["durable"]`. **That was a forecast recorded as an outcome, and it was rejected.** `record` is synchronous and returns before the writer has touched SQLite; nothing synchronous can honestly say `durable`. The vocabulary is therefore **admission, never disk**: `"queued"` (accepted into an open durable stream — the healthy path, suppressed), `"in-memory-only"`, `"absent"`, `"unconfirmed"`. The record carries `detail["stream"]`, not `detail["durable"]`: a record cannot attest its own durability, and what does attest it is the presence of its row in SQLite. Waiting for the commit was considered and rejected — it would couple every execution's latency to a disk write and reverse `execution/audit.py`'s shipped reasoning — and amending the label afterwards is impossible, because the result has already been returned. **Both** execution paths surface a non-`"queued"` outcome in their own result: `ToolResult.output["audit"]` on the agentic path and `IntentResult.result["audit"]` on the mesh `CodeRunnerAgent` path. The two comparisons are one atomic edit — changing only one would emit a label on **every healthy run** of the other, which trains the Captain to ignore the field and fails as completely as never labelling. AD-1280's per-auditor absence sentinel is deliberately **not** collapsed onto a process-wide flag: two untrailed paths is two facts.

**The cost, stated plainly.** An operator who sets `audit_enabled: false`, or whose sink fails mid-run, **still gets code execution**. There remains a configuration in which ProbOS runs Python with no durable accountability trail. We accept that, and in exchange every such run is self-labelled as ungoverned in its own result and in its own record, on both paths, so the capability is never *silently* ungoverned. The residual risk is an operator who reads neither. A runtime that refuses to execute because a SQLite file is locked costs more than it buys, and would not have saved the record anyway.

**The eviction trap, and the mechanism that avoids it.** `verify_chain()` walks from `GENESIS_HASH`; evicting `entries[0]` makes it return `False`. A bounded log would therefore report itself as **tampered** on every boot, and boot would log "tamper or corruption suspected" for a log that is merely full — getting the cap without this would be worse than not getting the cap, because it makes the control lie in the most damaging direction, crying tamper until nobody believes it. So eviction advances an **anchored genesis**, `_truncated_at = (sequence, entry_hash)` of the last entry dropped, and `verify_chain()` walks from there. Truncation is not tampering, so a correctly truncated chain still verifies `True`; the richer answer is a second accessor, `chain_state() -> (state, first_sequence, evicted_count)`, which never reports `"intact"` once a watermark exists. The watermark is **forward-only and raises on a backwards write** — an anchor a caller could move freely would let tampering masquerade as truncation, pointing the anchor at the break so a mutated chain verifies as intact.

**The persisted sequence stream must never gain a hole, and the fix is at the source rather than in the bookkeeping.** The first attempt bounded memory with a single `max(confirmed)` watermark and dropped an entry that could not enter the write queue. Measured against real SQLite: `db [0, 3]`, `mem [2, 3]`, in-memory `verify True` but rehydrated `verify False` / `("broken", 0, 0)`. **The eviction bug was the smaller half.** `AuditEntry.prior_hash` chains each row to its predecessor, so a sequence that never reaches the sink leaves the *next* persisted row pointing at a row that is not there — the durable artefact is poisoned permanently, and reports `broken` at every future boot. Every candidate that only taught the watermark to be careful would have left that injury in place. There are **two** hole sources and the second survives a perfect queue: `persist_entries` is all-or-nothing, so a writer that skips a refused batch lets the *next* success confirm a higher range than the failure. So: overflow **spills** into a FIFO buffer the writer drains behind the queue rather than dropping; a refused batch is **retried in place** (one writer means in-place *is* head-of-stream) and, after `audit_write_max_retries` consecutive failures, the durable stream **terminates** — nothing further is written, so the chain **ends cleanly instead of gaining a gap**, and `durable_stream_open()` is `False` from that moment so every later run self-labels. Terminating rather than limping is the deliberate trade: a chain with a hole lies about its own integrity for ever, while one that stops says plainly where it ended. Recovery needs a restart. And `mark_persisted_through` **refuses a non-contiguous advance outright**, logging at ERROR, with the writer stepping one sequence at a time over the confirmed run. That guard is kept even though the spill and the retry make a hole unreachable by construction — *"unreachable by construction"* is precisely what the previous revision's seventeen-mutant matrix believed, and one comparison converts a design argument into a runtime invariant.

**The cap is a memory bound, never a data-destruction policy — and the policy splits on whether durability was ever promised.** An undifferentiated refusal to evict was also rejected: with persistence off, `_persisted_through` stays `-1` for ever, so nothing is evictable and `audit_max_entries` is **decorative in the commonest deployment** — the memory bound quietly not existing. So with **no sink attached** the log is a ring buffer *by the operator's choice*, eviction is normal FIFO, and the truncation watermark keeps the remainder verifiable; nobody was promised a durable copy, so there is no only-copy-on-disk to protect. With a sink **attached and behind**, nothing above the watermark is touched and pressure is logged instead — an entry somebody was told would be durable, and which is not yet durable, is the one thing eviction must never destroy. That gate is only sound because the confirmed stream is contiguous: a durability gate reading a watermark that stepped over a hole would delete precisely the entries it exists to protect.

**Boot had to learn the same thing.** `load_entries()` gained a bound (`limit`, newest rows in ascending order) plus `watermark_before()`, and `finalize` anchors **before** it verifies — a bounded rehydrate legitimately does not start at genesis, and verifying it unanchored reports a full log as tampered. `append` also stopped deriving its sequence from `len(entries)`, which eviction falsifies.

**The drain is bounded at 2.0s on its own field, and runs in two phases.** `shutdown_drain_timeout_s` (30.0) is deliberately not reused — it is larger than the 10s `__main__.py` allows the *whole* teardown, so borrowing it would guarantee the audit drain is cancelled from outside rather than completing. `asyncio.wait` rather than `asyncio.wait_for`: on timeout `wait_for` cancels the inner task and then awaits it **unbounded**, so a writer that caught `CancelledError` to finish a final commit would hang shutdown forever. `flush()` was unbounded and is now bounded the same way, for the same reason. **Two phases, because `drain()` closes registration.** A single drain placed with the other stores ran ~138 lines before the pool scaler, the pools and intent bus, the knowledge store, the mesh services and the semantic layer — every one of which can produce an audit-worthy event, in the most failure-prone stretch of the run, which is where a durability control is least allowed to be absent. So phase 1 is a **bounded flush that leaves registration open**, at the store-teardown site, on half the budget; phase 2 is the authoritative drain, placed after `_semantic_layer.stop()` and before `runtime._started = False`, which is the last point at which anything can append, and above the deferred-cancellation re-raise so a cancellation carried over from pool teardown cannot skip it. On expiry the loss is stated at ERROR with the unflushed count and the unconfirmed sequence range; on cancellation the writer is cancelled and the error re-raised, because cancellation belongs to the shutdown.

**Three false claims corrected in the same change as the behaviour they describe** — not before, because a docstring promising durability the code has not got yet is the identical defect pointing the other way. `execution/audit.py` called the record "the control that makes the capability defensible" with **zero** hedges anywhere in the module (verified by the same enumeration the issue ran); `security/audit.py` still said "v1 in-memory only … Persistence to SQLite deferred to AD-456d" with `AuditLogPersistence` 130 lines below it, and `AuditLogPersistence.stop()` still said it was unwired; and `shutdown.py` said `__main__.py` "enforces a 5s timeout on stop()" when it is 10s (the 5s bounds `adapter.stop()`, a different call). A fourth was introduced by the first attempt at this AD and corrected here: the `audit_log` schema comment claimed `sequence` was "already monotonic per `len(self.entries)`-based assignment", contradicting the `_next_sequence()` comment 130 lines above it, which says the opposite because eviction breaks that identity.

**Deliberately not built.** No second audit path for execution — `AuditLog` is shared and the AD-706 browser tool and the approval gate gain equally. No consensus gate on `run_python`; BF-763 settled that and this AD is the other half of that bargain, not a reversal. No change to `AuditEntry` (frozen, and its six fields are the hash payload). No change to `verify_chain()`'s signature. No retention or TTL on the SQLite rows — the cap bounds memory only, and disk retention stays open.

### AD-1282 (2026-08-28) - verification outcome attribution belongs to the session path (BF-782, #1246)

BF-778 removed the trust write from `SubtaskVerifier.verify()` — it recorded the verifier with `success=verdict.accepted`, which paid a judge to agree and charged it for every refusal, inverting the point of an adversarial layer. It left `record_verification_outcome` behind as a seam "adjudication will call", and #1246 asked which path should call it. **The answer is that no path should, because the capability already exists elsewhere, implemented better.**

**The enumeration that decides it.** Attributing a resolved refusal requires three things at once: seeing the refusal, re-running the producer, and retaining the round history long enough to attribute the outcome. `crew_orchestrator._verify()` → `verify()` is live but single-shot — it builds `ConvergenceOutcome(..., rounds=0)` and never re-runs, so it has no resolution to observe. `SubtaskVerifier.converge()` re-runs and re-verifies but keeps its history in local variables and has **zero production callers** (verified by enumeration: `.converge(` matches only `test_ad860_crew_verifier.py` and `test_bf777_bf778_verifier_trust.py`). Only `converge_for_session` both retains `history: list[SessionVerificationRound]` and runs in production, from `crew_finalizer.py:1315` and `:2092`. It already credits the resolution: `crew_trust.derive_completed_crew_trust_effects` pays a round where `verdict["status"] == "refuted" and index + 1 < len(child.rounds)` — "a refusal with a later round after it" **is** "a refusal a correction resolved" — and delivery runs through the durable outbox to `TrustNetwork.record_outcome_once`, keyed on an `outcome_id` derived from the evidence hash and revision.

**The issue's premise was wrong, and the correction matters.** #1246 states that BF-778 moved attribution "into `converge()`, which credits a refusal once a correction resolves it." `converge()` credits nothing. BF-778 removed the `verify()` write and deliberately did not add one; the comment block inside `converge()` records that an earlier revision tried exactly that and it was rejected as farmable by a whitespace edit.

**Rejected: emit the resolution from the session path as well.** That path is already the emitter. A second write pays the same verifier twice for one judgement, and it would bypass the outbox's idempotency rather than being deduplicated by it, because the outbox only dedupes what passes through it.

**Rejected: give `converge()` a production caller.** That means giving the legacy orchestrator a re-run loop — a change to *admission*, which BF-778 scoped out. The repo had already recorded this boundary twice, unprompted: `crew_executor.py:199` ("READ THIS BEFORE ADDING A THIRD OUTER LOOP. **One already exists.**") and `config.py:7231`.

**So the seam is deleted rather than stubbed.** `record_verification_outcome` had no callable position — from the session path it double-credits, and from the legacy path there is no resolution signal to give it. A named seam invites a caller, and this one had already done measurable harm: while it existed unused, three shipped comments came to assert that a caller existed, one of them (`crew_verifier.py:1144`) naming the convergence path outright while `crew_synth.py:537` simultaneously said it had none. A docstring claiming a property the code does not provide is the defect class this repo flags; here the source contradicted *itself* across two modules. No deprecation shim was left, for the same reason.

**No production behaviour changes.** The deleted method was unreachable, and the trust writes before and after are identical. What changes is that the documentation now describes the path that actually runs.

**The test that was owed.** The existing coverage stopped short in both directions: `test_ad1130_outcome_only_room_trust.py::test_completed_derivation_rewards_corrected_producer_and_verifiers` exercises the derive function with a hand-built round history and never crosses the `converge_for_session` seam, and the finalizer-level test in the same file asserts only that the verifier's alpha exceeds 3.0 — which the accepted round alone satisfies. Neither discriminates the credit for the **refusal**, which is the entire decision. `test_ad1282_verifier_credit_full_chain.py` drives the production entry point through every seam to a real `TrustNetwork` and identifies the refusal credit by its own `outcome_id` in the delivered outbox, so the acceptance credit landing instead cannot satisfy it. Confirmed discriminating by a single targeted mutant on the refuted arm of `correct_judgment`, which the test kills.

**Deliberately untouched: the `verdict["status"] == "accepted"` half of that predicate.** Whether a plain acceptance should pay at all is the acceptance-incentive question and belongs to BF-783 (#1247).

### AD-1279 (2026-08-27) - the trace carries the fault's identity (BF-855, #1325)

AD-1269 made a fault row's signature the identity computed **once at detection**, over the untruncated error — `ToolDefect.__post_init__` says *"ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING"* in capitals, because deriving the key after truncation split one detected defect into two durable rows with `occurrences [1, 1]`. But `find_failing_arguments` **recomputed** that signature from the *persisted* trace, and `build_tool_trace_payload` head+tail truncates each output before writing it. When the two disagreed, argument recovery returned `None` and a fault filed correctly, coalesced correctly, with the right `tool_id` and `observed_as`, could **never enter the repair path**.

**The precondition the issue did not state, and it decides the test.** `normalise_error` collapses hex runs, then digit runs, and only **then** truncates to `_ERROR_MAX = 2000`; head+tail truncation preserves the head. So when the collapsed head is already ≥ 2000 characters the first 2000 collapsed characters are identical either way and **the two signatures agree**. Length alone is not the trigger. Measured on the real writer and the real reader, `_durable_head_tail(8192, …) → head 5358`: a 34-character control recovered; a 25,800-character error with a *wordy* head collapsed to exactly 2000 and recovered; an 11,671-character error with a 5,400-digit run **in the head** collapsed to **4** characters and did not. A first probe built its long error from a repeating pattern, got a collapse-resistant head, and **wrongly refuted the issue** — so the fixture matrix is single-dimension by construction, and the dense case is retained as a boundary fixture so a future change to `_ERROR_MAX` or the head/tail split cannot silently widen or close the defect.

**D1 — a trace entry may carry a second identity: `error_signature`, on error entries only.** The mechanism was not invented here. `build_tool_trace_payload`'s own docstring establishes that readers version by **key presence**, and `source_chars` was added exactly that way for BF-760. AD-1269's do-not-build #12 objected to forking provenance by adding a second **name**; a digest is not a name. The entry gains no `tool_id`, `canonical_tool_id` or `observed_as` key, so `name` remains what the model used and the fault row still owns the canonical id. Success entries are untouched, so every non-error blob is byte-identical, and `output_max_chars == 0` still yields the pre-AD-1151 blob because no result is joined at all.

**D2 — readers version by key presence, and recomputation is retained, not replaced.** The fallback is taken on a **mismatch** as well as on absence. The writer and the detector each canonicalise through an injected resolver that is `None` when there is no registry; a skew between them would otherwise make the field authoritative *and wrong*. Recomputation cannot produce a false positive against a specific 256-bit target except by collision, so keeping it is strictly more permissive and costs nothing. Legacy traces therefore resolve exactly as before and there is nothing to migrate.

**D3 — the signature is computed in the writer, by calling `error_signature`.** `ToolDefect.signature` documents itself as byte-identical to that function, and BF-856 already collapsed their hashing onto a shared `_digest` because *"two parallel edits can drift; a shared definition cannot."* A third implementation would reintroduce the risk that helper exists to remove, so `_canonical_tool_id` was promoted to public `canonical_tool_id` rather than copied — the caller set was exactly one internal site, with no test importing the private name and no alias left behind.

**The seam is the coercion, and it is the easiest thing here to get wrong.** The writer renders a `None` output as `""`; the detector renders it as `"None"`. Signing the writer's value would make the two disagree on exactly the malformed-result case the writer's own comment says is reachable — so the signature material uses the detector's coercion while `original`, which feeds `output_chars` and the persisted output, is left alone.

**D4 — rejected: make the detector sign what will be persisted.** Recorded so it is not re-proposed. AD-1269 already measured truncate-then-normalise as a different identity and chose against it. The decisive reason is stronger: the detector **cannot** know what will be persisted, even in principle. Beyond per-output truncation, the writer performs whole-blob tail elision, so an entry's output can be replaced by `""` because of how many *other* tools were called in the same turn. Signing the persisted form would make a fault's identity depend on unrelated traffic — the same fault would key differently in a busy turn and a quiet one, and AD-1169 coalescing would break. That is not a trade-off; it is a correctness loss. The asymmetry is closed by making the trace carry the detector's identity, never by moving the detector to the trace's.

**One resolver object, not two calls.** `WorkItemAgenticExecutor.run` builds `_tool_id_resolver(registry)` once and hands the same object to the writer and to the detector. Two calls would close over the same registry and answer identically today; one object makes "the writer and the detector cannot disagree" a property of the code rather than of the resolver's current implementation.

**Folded in: `FaultReportStore.start()` had no exception guard.** It connected, ran the schema, migrated and loaded the cache with no `try`, so a failing post-connect step left the aiosqlite connection open and its worker thread alive — measured as **pytest hanging indefinitely rather than failing**, which is a hazard to the very gate that has to prove the rest of this AD. It now closes and re-raises, with the close itself guarded so a failing close cannot mask the original cause. **Propagate, not log-and-degrade:** a store that came up with an empty cache would silently re-file every recurring fault as new, which is a data-integrity failure wearing a degradation costume.

### AD-1165 (2026-07-30) - a conversational turn that outgrows a reply becomes a task

Asked to type into his open document, Ezri answered `(error: Agent did not respond in time.)` — on a turn in which she was working correctly. A Captain DM is dispatched with `ttl_seconds=60.0` and `IntentBus` enforces it as `wait_for(handler(intent), timeout=...)`, so AD-1065's conversational loop runs *inside* that deadline. BF-692 and BF-697 had just made the browser work real enough to take five iterations at ~9s each; `max_iterations` was raised 5 → 10 without anyone noticing the enclosing 60s. Ten iterations do not fit in sixty seconds, and never will.

**The fix I proposed first was wrong and is recorded because the correction is the decision.** I wanted the TTL to measure *progress* rather than duration. The Captain's answer: *"we came up with a structure where we could have a TTL for chat based requests and then the concept of the agent creating tasks that could run in the background async and allow me to keep chatting."* The architecture already existed and was designed for exactly this. A bigger or cleverer ceiling trades one arbitrary number for another and makes a genuinely hung turn hold the chat open for longer. **The 60s TTL is correct and is untouched.** What was wrong is that a *reply* and *work* were the same object. They are not, so work that does not fit inside a reply stops being one.

**Promotion is decided by elapsed evidence, never by classification.** There is no "is this task-shaped?" model call and no keyword heuristic — a turn is promoted precisely because it *has already* run past the budget, which is the only signal that cannot be wrong about the thing it measures. A fast turn returns before the timer is consulted, so `promote_to_task_after_seconds: 0` (the shipped default) and any turn under the budget are byte-identical to AD-1164.

**The in-flight run is never cancelled or restarted.** Promotion stops *waiting* for the `asyncio.Task`; it does not touch it. The same run continues with its full message history, its tool trace and every side effect it has already produced. A design that cancelled and re-dispatched through `WorkItemRouter` would replay every click and every keystroke the agent had already performed — for browser work, the exact hazard this AD exists to unblock. For the same reason the promoted item is deliberately **not dispatchable**: no `metadata["dispatchable"]`, and its tag is asserted disjoint from `hybrid_dispatch.dispatchable_tags`, so nothing executes it a second time. The item is the durable *record* of work in flight, not a request for someone to start it.

**Nothing new was built.** `WorkItemStore` opens the row and moves it `open → in_progress → done|failed` through the real AD-498 state machine; `ChatThreadStore.append_message` posts the report; and the report reaches the Captain's open transcript with **zero UI change** because AD-1133 already emits `CHAT_THREAD_MESSAGE_APPENDED` on commit and `ProfileChatTab` already refreshes on it. This is the era's defect shape read backwards: every mechanism existed, was correct, and was tested — and the caller never reached for it.

**Every failure degrades to the inline wait, never past it.** No thread to report into, no work-item store, a store that raises — each falls back to awaiting the run under today's TTL. Acknowledging without a durable destination would promise a report that nothing delivers, which is worse than the error it replaces. A failed `in_progress` transition still promotes and still reports (a wrong board row must not cost the Captain the work), a raising thread store still closes the item and writes the report to the log rather than dropping it, and a *cancelled* run leaves the item `in_progress` — cancellation means unfinished, and stamping a terminal status would tell the board a completed story about work that simply stopped.

Two details worth keeping. The budget is read through an exact `type` check rather than a bare `getattr`: every synthetic-runtime test builds the config as a `MagicMock`, which auto-creates the attribute as a truthy proxy whose comparisons return another mock, so the arming decision would have been made on something that is not a number — the same phantom-attribute trap AD-1062 hit with `system_trigger`. And the work item records the Captain's **raw** message, not the assembled prompt, which carries working memory, episodic recall and session history and would make a board row unreadable.

The acknowledgement and both report lines are checked against the real `_CAPABILITY_GAP_RE`. A match there would route a routine "I've started on that" into the self-modification pipeline every time a turn ran long.

### AD-1164 (2026-07-29) - the step limit becomes a checkpoint that asks

When the conversational agentic loop exhausted `dm_agentic.max_iterations` it stopped dead. BF-697 had just fixed it *discarding* the work — the partial text now survives — but the agent still had no way to say "I was cut off", so **exhausting the budget was indistinguishable from finishing**. Measured on the vessel: asked to type into a document, the agent spent its five iterations on `state, screenshot, click, click, click`, never reached `key_type`, and reported as though the turn were over. Raising the ceiling to 10 was the stopgap; this is the structural fix. GitHub Copilot's model is the shape being copied — a budget ceiling is a checkpoint that asks, not a cliff that truncates.

**Almost nothing here is new, and that is the design.** AD-1155 already built re-invocation for the crew fan-out, so `_REINVOKABLE_STOPPED_REASONS` and `_render_continuation` are **imported** from `crew_executor`, which is not modified at all — the membership set keeps its single member and AD-1155's deliberate exclusions hold unchanged (`token_budget` is an operator's spend ceiling, `error` is usually window exhaustion that a longer prompt makes *worse*, `complete` means the model chose to stop). AD-853's `CapabilityRequestStore` is the durable queue, reached through a **fifth kind**, `"continue"` — a fifth kind rather than a second store for AD-1154's reason verbatim, and the AD-857 REST surface, the Captain-DM notifier and the kind-agnostic HXI panel all render it with no change, re-verified rather than assumed. AD-1154's `ActionApprovalStore` is the standing-rule mechanism: no second store, no second TTL, and no wildcard — `scope_key` is empty because continuation is scoped by `agent_id` ("let Ezri keep going"), and an empty scope matches only an empty scope.

**The `(tool_id, action, scope_key)` triple doubles as the persisted payload**, in AD-1154's exact six-key shape, so the row survives a restart through `_decode_payload`'s re-validation instead of degrading to `None`. A cache-only store never runs that path, so the suite uses real SQLite for it.

**Known limit, stated rather than left to be discovered from a silent branch.** The only production caller of `issue_approval` is `_maybe_issue_standing_rule`, gated on `kind == "action"`, and this AD does not touch the decide endpoint. So nothing *issues* a `kind="continue"` standing rule at HEAD and the re-invocation branch is reachable only through the store's public API. That is AD-1159's precedent — ship the consult, wire the issuance next — and given how many times this era has shipped a mechanism nothing exercises, it is recorded here in the same breath as the feature rather than a paragraph later. **What is live today is the half that matters**: a cut-off turn files a durable ask and says plainly that it stopped mid-task.

**Fail-safe in exactly one direction.** An absent store, a raising cache read, a continuation that will not compose, a re-invocation that throws — every one degrades to today's behaviour: stop, and report the partial work. An approval mechanism must never be able to fail a run that would otherwise return something, so the worst a bug here can do is ask the Captain a question they did not need.

The cut-off text is checked against the real `_CAPABILITY_GAP_RE` (the natural phrasing for "I did not finish" reaches straight for "could not" and "unable to", and `lack` is a bare substring) **and** against reading as a completion — a note that says the work is done defeats the entire point. `continue_or_ask_max_passes` counts total passes including the first and ships at 2, mirroring `crew_loop_until_done_max_iterations` so the two bounds mean the same thing.

### AD-1163 (2026-07-28) - tell the agent the Captain's browser session exists

AD-1158 bound the session through the call context; AD-1162 supplied the binding. Both correct, both tested. Live result: Ezri, holding a `write` grant on `browser`, offered the tool, and bound to the Captain's exact session, made **zero tool calls** and replied that she could not interact with applications on the Captain's machine.

She was reasoning correctly from what she knew. AD-1158's own entry states the design intent: *"The binding travels through the call context, so no prompt text and no model accuracy is involved."* That was right for reliability — no UUID has to survive a model copying it — but invisible to the plumbing turned out to mean invisible to the agent. She saw a tool described as "drive a Chromium browser" and a request about "the document I have open", and nothing connected them.

So the offered description now names the page: *"A browser session is already open and shared with the Captain showing 'Document 5.docx'. When the Captain refers to a page or document they have open, that is this session. Omit session_id and your call acts on it."* Same fix shape as BF-690 — make the offer honest about what is actually available. It composes with BF-690's read-only narrowing (both only rewrite `function.description`), and the text is checked against the real `_CAPABILITY_GAP_RE`, since phrasing that reads as a capability gap would defeat the purpose.

**This extends the defect family in a way the existing forcing question would not have caught.** "Name the real caller" was satisfied — AD-1162 *is* the caller. Producer and reader were both wired and both correct. What was missing is that the **consumer who must decide to invoke the capability was never told it existed.** For anything an agent chooses to use rather than something the runtime calls on its behalf, wiring the mechanism is necessary and not sufficient; the agent has to be able to know it is there.

Also adds the line whose absence cost two diagnostic cycles: when the browser is offered and **no** Captain session is bound, that now logs explicitly. Previously the only evidence was a *missing* INFO line, which is invisible unless you already suspect it — and reading a missing line as a second failed run is exactly the mistake that sent this investigation down two dead ends.

### AD-1162 (2026-07-28) - the producer for the session binding AD-1158 reads

AD-1158 taught `BrowserTool.invoke` to read `context["browser_session_id"]` so an agent acts on the session the Captain is watching rather than spawning a fresh, signed-out browser. **Nothing outside tests ever supplied that key.** The mechanism was inert: every agent browser call created a new session while the Captain watched a different one, and the demo it was built for would have silently typed into an invisible browser.

This is the same defect this era's preamble names — and it is the most instructive instance, because AD-1158's own test suite passed while the feature did nothing. Those tests construct the context dict themselves and assert `invoke` reads it. That proves the *reader*. It cannot prove a *producer* exists, and no amount of strengthening it would have. A test that supplies the very input it is meant to verify arrives from elsewhere is structurally incapable of detecting that nothing sends it.

`BrowserTool.captain_session_id` is the producer, and `WorkItemAgenticExecutor.run` supplies it into the loop context. Three decisions worth keeping:

**Only Captain-owned sessions bind.** `agent_id == "captain"` is set by `open_captain_session` (AD-1161); agent-opened sessions carry the agent's own id and are deliberately not bindable this way. An agent silently inheriting *another agent's* browser is a capability leak, not a convenience.

**It reads the public `list_sessions()`, not `self._sessions`.** The ownership rule then lives in exactly one place, and the property cannot drift from what the sessions API reports.

**Every failure direction degrades to `None`** — no browser tool, an older build without the property, a raising property. `None` restores AD-1158's behaviour exactly: the agent creates its own session. An ambient convenience must never be able to fail a run that would otherwise succeed.

Multiple live Captain sessions bind the most recent and warn, naming the count. Ambiguity there is real (the agent acts on one browser, not all of them) and silently picking is worse than saying so.

### BF-696 (2026-07-28) - a concurrent subscribe during the dispatch-consumer drain killed the boot

`IntentBus.create_dispatch_consumers` iterated `self._subscribers.items()` while awaiting `_js_subscribe_agent_dispatch` **inside** the loop. Every await yields to the event loop, so a concurrent `subscribe()` mutated the dict mid-iteration and raised `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` — which propagates out of `finalize_startup` and takes the entire boot down. Observed live at `finalize.py:4507`.

The live producer is the JetStream retry loop: `perception.vision_aggregator` re-subscribing after `nats: timeout` on a 0.5s/1.0s backoff. That failure has sat in every boot log for weeks as a recurring warning; what was not appreciated is that its retry can land inside the drain window and take the process with it. "Noisy warning" and "can kill startup" turned out to be the same defect wearing different clothes.

Fixed by snapshotting with `tuple(...)` before iterating. The snapshot is **complete**, not merely safe, and that distinction is the whole argument: `_defer_dispatch_consumers` is cleared at the top of the method with no intervening await, so any agent subscribing after that point creates its own dispatch consumer through the normal `subscribe()` path. Nobody is missed and nobody is created twice. A test pins that ordering specifically, because it is the property that makes the snapshot correct rather than merely non-crashing — reorder those two statements and the fix silently starts dropping consumers instead of raising.

### AD-1161 (2026-07-28) - the Captain can open a browser session

`GET /api/browser/sessions` **listed** sessions; nothing **created** one. A session came into existence only when an agent called `goto`, so the Captain could open the Browser workstation, switch to Watch, and find an empty picker with no way to say "open a page for me". The flow the Captain actually needs is the reverse ordering — *they* open the browser, sign into Word Online by hand, and only then hand the authenticated session to an agent. Nothing in the browser stack expressed that ordering.

**Navigation reuses `invoke({"action": "goto"})` rather than a private path.** `domain_allowlist`, `domain_denylist`, the tier classification and the AD-706 audit row all bind at that one seam; a hand-rolled navigate would have had to re-implement each of them, and each re-implementation is a place they can drift apart. Nothing about a Captain-initiated open is exempt from browser policy — only the *initiator* differs, which is why `agent_id` defaults to `"captain"` and shows up in `list_sessions()` and every audit row.

**A refused navigation must not strand a live session.** `invoke` creates the session *before* the domain gate runs, so the refusal path holds a started Chromium nothing else would ever close — the reaper only sweeps on expiry, up to `session_max_duration_seconds` later. `open_captain_session` discards it explicitly and emits `BROWSER_SESSION_CLOSED{reason: "open_failed"}` so a discarded session is indistinguishable from an expired one to any consumer. The discard is keyed on the `session_id` in `ToolResult.metadata`, not on a before/after set difference of `_sessions`: a concurrent open would appear in that difference and be closed out from under its owner.

**No `confirm` parameter, deliberately.** `connect_bridge_session` needs one because it attaches to an already-authenticated browser the Captain did not open for this purpose — the consent is about handing over existing credentials. Opening a fresh session is the Captain acting on their own surface with nothing yet in it; a confirmation there is friction with no matching risk. A test asserts the parameter's absence so this is not "hardened" later by analogy to the bridge.

**The workstation now defaults to Watch, not Embedded.** Embedded is an `<iframe>`, and every target worth opening — Word Online, OneDrive, most SaaS — sends `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors` and refuses to render in one. Landing the Captain on a mode that structurally cannot show the thing they came for is the wrong default. The mode is resolved from the `enabled` flag on the sessions probe the watch surface already calls, not a second capability endpoint, and the probe is mount-only: once the Captain picks a mode by hand nothing may move it under them.

`_BROWSER_LOOP_ACTIONS` is byte-identical and asserted so. `classify_action`, the action handlers and `_action_state` (BF-692) are untouched.

**Spec correction.** The build prompt credited the `goto` path with "scheme validation" and a "session cap"; neither exists. `_check_domain` parses a host and returns "allowed" when there isn't one, so `file:///` and `javascript:` reach `page.goto` unfiltered, and `_get_or_create_session` counts nothing. Both predate this AD and both apply to agents today, so neither is fixed here — the UI's existing `_normalizeUrl` blocks dangerous schemes on the Captain's path only. Filed for the Architect rather than widened into this AD.


Word Online draws its document into `<div id="WACViewPanel">`: no `contenteditable`, no input element, no accessible role anywhere in the document body. Every element-scoped path fails there by construction — `_action_type` does `page.fill(selector, text)` and there is nothing fillable; `_action_click` needs a selector `state` cannot supply. The primitives that *do* work were verified by hand against a live document: move the mouse into the canvas, click, then `keyboard.type(text, delay=...)`. AD-1052c's `forward_input` already uses exactly those for the *human* path; the agent path could not reach them.

**BF-693 — `mouse_button` clicked the wrong place.** The handler ended `await mouse.click(0, 0, button=button) if not hasattr(mouse, "click_button") else await mouse.click_button(button)`. Playwright's `Mouse` has **no `click_button` method**, so the `hasattr` was always False and every `action="click"` clicked viewport **(0, 0)** while the docstring promised "at the current position". `mouse_move(x, y)` followed by `mouse_button(action="click")` moved to the target and clicked the top-left corner. Now `mouse.down()` + `mouse.up()` — the correct idiom for clicking where the mouse already is, needing no coordinates and no new session state. The dead `click_button` branch is deleted rather than left as a guard against a method that does not exist.

**AD-1160 — `key_type`.** Types free text at the current keyboard focus, no selector, mirroring `forward_input`'s `kind == "type"` branch. `delay_ms` is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: a canvas app drops keystrokes typed at full speed, which is why the manual verification needed ~90 ms. Validation is log-and-degrade, not raise — the delay only tunes cadence, so a malformed value should still land the keystrokes; refusing the whole action over it would be the less honest outcome. `bool` is rejected explicitly (`isinstance(True, int)` is `True`, and `delay=True` would reach Playwright as a silent 1 ms), as are negatives and anything above a 250 ms ceiling, since delay × len(text) holds the event loop for minutes on a long string. Classified in `classify_action` exactly as `type` is — tier 2 ordinary, tier 3 on tier-3 domains/paths/element text — never tier 1, because it mutates.

**A drift guard, from BF-690's lesson.** The tool description claimed a "10-action vocabulary" while the enum held 11. A test now asserts the stated count equals the actual enum length, so the description cannot silently disagree with the schema again.

**Adjacent, filed not fixed.** `_action_state` guards on `hasattr(page, "list_elements")` — a method real Playwright's `Page` does not have — so `state` has returned an empty element list against every real page since AD-706 shipped, and the entire index-based `click`/`type` flow has never functioned in production. Its tests pass because they inject a fake page implementing the method. That is **BF-692**; this AD deliberately routes around element discovery rather than depending on it, and leaves `_action_state` untouched. `_BROWSER_LOOP_ACTIONS` is byte-identical and asserted so.

### AD-1159 (2026-07-27) - the work permit: a durable, single-holder authorization to act on a workstation

The naval Permit to Work applied to a crew session. One agent, authorized by a *different* agent, to act on one workstation, up to a bounded hazard tier, until an explicit expiry. **Nothing consumes it in this AD** — AD-1154's precedent, verbatim: shipping a gate together with the actions it gates means the gate's first exercise is in production. AD-1160 wires it.

**Why a fifth store rather than widening one of the four.** `ToolPermissionStore` keys on `(agent_id, tool_id, permission)` and `IntentGrantStore` on `(agent_id, intent_name)` — both are **capability** grants (*may this agent hold this tool*), with no session, no workstation, no occupancy. `ActionApprovalStore` keys on `(agent_id, tool_id, action, scope_key)` — an **action** grant, and deliberately additive: two approvals for the same shape coexist harmlessly. A permit is an **occupancy** grant — *this agent, and no other, holds this space right now* — so its defining property is mutual exclusion, which no additive store can provide without changing the meaning of every existing row. The new store mirrors `ActionApprovalStore` structurally (`ConnectionFactory` injection, WAL, `busy_timeout=5000`, in-memory cache for zero-I/O sync reads, lazy expiry on read rather than a reaper), making it the fifth instance of one pattern rather than a fifth pattern.

**Four load-bearing invariants.** *Single holder* — at most one open, unexpired permit per `(session_id, workstation_id)`; a second issue raises `PermitConflict` rather than silently superseding, because a permit that vanishes because somebody else asked is the exact failure PTW exists to prevent. *Issuing authority is not performing authority* — `issued_by == holder_id` is rejected; the crew's standing orders already state this as prose (`surgeon.md`: "Every operation must have CMO authorization or Captain approval"; `yeoman.md`: "you do not issue orders on your own authority"), and here it is enforced. *`expires_at` is `NOT NULL` in the schema*, not merely in the signature — `ttl_seconds` is required and there is deliberately no `expires_at: float | None` overload, so the invariant is carried by the type system as well as the column. *No wildcards on the authorization path* — `""` matches only `""`.

**`ttl_seconds` validation is not decoration.** A non-positive TTL produced a permit that was born inert and still returned a `WorkPermit` reporting success — a success-shaped no-op, the same class AD-1154 exists to eliminate. It would have become actively dangerous in AD-1161, where a transfer computing a *remaining* TTL can legitimately go non-positive and would have read as a successful handoff granting nothing. Rejected now: non-real, non-finite, `<= 0`, and `bool` (`isinstance(True, int)` is `True`, so `max_tier=True` would otherwise silently mean tier 1). Expiry is exercised through an **injected clock** (`clock: Callable[[], float] = time.time`, the `CrewSessionService` precedent) rather than by fabricating permits with negative TTLs — deterministic, and it tests expiry the way expiry actually happens.

**Known bound, stated rather than hidden.** The single-holder check reads the in-memory cache, authoritative for one process after `start()`. Two processes over one database file could both pass and both insert. A partial unique index on `(session_id, workstation_id) WHERE closed = 0` was considered and rejected: it would also reject an *expired* open row and so contradict lazy expiry. Every sibling store shares this single-writer assumption.

**Naval prior art checked before building, and mostly found dormant.** `NightOrdersManager` is instantiated but nothing dispatches it; `NIGHT_ORDER_TEMPLATES` has zero call sites; all `WatchManager` state is in-memory and lost on restart, and it is only constructed when `proactive_cognitive.enabled`. So watch-turnover revalidation — the naval answer to bounding a session that stalls rather than closes — is **deliberately not built here**, because coupling permits to an unrelated flag and to unpersisted state would be worse than deferring it.
